> **The forgotten skill of navigation**
> 
> **A.** For most of human history, finding one’s way was a skill acquired in childhood and refined throughout life. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean using swell patterns, star positions and the flight paths of birds, without instruments of any kind. European sailors developed different but equally demanding methods. In both traditions, the knowledge was held collectively and transmitted through years of apprenticeship.
> 
> **B.** Satellite navigation has made these skills unnecessary for ordinary purposes, and their disappearance has been rapid. Surveys of drivers under thirty in several countries find that a majority report difficulty reaching an unfamiliar destination without turn-by-turn instructions. This is not surprising, and by itself would matter little; few now regret the loss of skill in operating a manual telephone exchange.
> 
> **C.** What has attracted attention is a possible cognitive consequence. The hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory, is also central to spatial representation. Studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorise a vast street network before qualifying, found measurable enlargement of parts of this structure, with the effect increasing according to years of experience. The reverse question — whether reliance on satellite navigation reduces such capacity — has proved much harder to answer.
> 
> **D.** Some evidence is suggestive. Participants who navigate using turn-by-turn instructions show lower activity in the relevant regions and, when tested afterwards, remember the route less well than those who used a map. Whether this translates into any lasting change is unknown; the studies are short and the samples small.
> 
> **E.** A more cautious conclusion is available. What the research reliably shows is not that technology damages the brain but that we remember what we actively construct. A route followed by instruction is not built into a mental map, because no map was required. This is a claim about attention rather than harm, and it applies equally to any activity where the effort of organising information is handed to a machine.

> **Insurance and the invention of the future**
> 
> Marine insurance existed in Italian ports by the fourteenth century, but its logic remained limited for three hundred years: a merchant paid a sum, and if a ship was lost, he was compensated. Whether the price charged bore any relation to the actual risk was largely a matter of judgement and reputation.
> 
> The change came from an unexpected direction. In the seventeenth century, mathematicians studying games of chance developed methods for calculating the likelihood of future events. Applied to human lifespans, using the first reliable mortality records, these methods made it possible to price a promise about the future with reasonable accuracy. The first life assurance society founded on such calculations opened in London in 1762; earlier attempts, based on guesswork, had generally collapsed.
> 
> The consequences extended well beyond commerce. If risks could be measured, they could be compared, and a distinction emerged between misfortunes that were unpredictable and those that were, in a statistical sense, expected. Industrial accidents provide the clearest example. Once it was established that a factory of a given size would produce a predictable number of injuries each year, the argument that any particular injury was the worker’s own carelessness became difficult to sustain. Employers’ liability laws followed in most industrial countries within a few decades.
> 
> Historians disagree about how much weight to give this. Some treat statistical thinking as the decisive factor; others argue that trade unions and political pressure would have produced similar laws regardless, and that mathematics supplied a justification rather than a cause. What is not disputed is that the language changed. Events once described as acts of God came to be described as rates.

speaking.de_tom_tat: Reading tốc độ — Part 1 và Part 3 về đọc và thông tin.

cau_tra_loi.mau: Less than I'd like. Mostly work-related material and news during the week, then a book at weekends if I have the time.
cau_tra_loi.ghi_chu: "Less than I'd like" — trả lời trung thực có sắc thái, hay hơn "yes, a lot".

cau_tra_loi.hoi: Part 1 — Do you prefer paper books or e-books?
cau_tra_loi.mau: Paper, for anything I want to remember. I retain far more from a printed page, oddly enough. E-books are more practical when travelling, though.
cau_tra_loi.ghi_chu: Nêu tiêu chí phân biệt ("anything I want to remember") thay vì chọn chung chung.

cau_tra_loi.hoi: Part 3 — Are people reading less than they used to?
cau_tra_loi.mau: Reading less deeply, I'd say, rather than reading less overall. We probably read more words per day than any previous generation — but mostly in fragments. Sustained attention on a long argument is what's declining.
cau_tra_loi.ghi_chu: Tinh chỉnh chính câu hỏi ("less deeply rather than less overall") — kỹ thuật band cao.

cau_tra_loi.hoi: Part 3 — Should schools still teach reading of long texts?
cau_tra_loi.mau: More than ever, I'd argue. If nobody can follow a complex argument for twenty pages, public debate suffers — you end up with policy decided by headlines. It's a skill that has to be trained deliberately, because nothing in daily life requires it any more.
cau_tra_loi.ghi_chu: Nêu hệ quả xã hội cụ thể ("policy decided by headlines") — lập luận có chiều sâu.

cham_diem.vi_sao: Trả lời có tiêu chí phân biệt và tinh chỉnh câu hỏi.
retain · in fragments · sustained attention · deliberately.
Reading less deeply rather than reading less overall · If nobody can follow… public debate suffers · It's a skill that has to be trained.

meo_noi: Tinh chỉnh câu hỏi ("X rather than Y") là cách nhanh nhất thể hiện tư duy sắc — nhưng phải đúng.
Nêu hệ quả cụ thể ("policy decided by headlines") thay vì nói chung "nó không tốt".
"More than ever, I'd argue" — mở đầu dứt khoát, thu hút chú ý giám khảo.
